name: Dana Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Dana, thanks for your time. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you say is confidential, so tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm first-line support for a company that makes accounting software for small businesses, so cafés, builders, hairdressers. They chat or call when their invoices won't send or the bank feed stops matching. I've been there eight months. I use an AI assistant all day, I've even built my own list of prompts for the common problems.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the moment a café owner who's been fighting the software for an hour finally sees her numbers line up. What's hard is the accounting itself, because I'm not an accountant. Anything about tax or payroll, I escalate, and my manager says I escalate too much. My partner Rhys teaches PE, so at dinner he talks about football and I talk about bank feeds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? That would surprise me. But okay, I can play along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a good tool that got sold as magic. At work I'd tell people to keep using it for the boring bits. Online I'd probably share a funny post about all the AI startups going bust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. The AI I already use makes me faster, and if it stops getting better, I'm still ahead of the people who never learned it. My job feels pretty safe if the company keeps growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep refining my prompt list and share it with the team, maybe get some credit for it. I'd do a short bookkeeping course online so I escalate less. I'd keep saving like normal, about four months put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored by the idea, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're ahead of people who never learned it. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a guy on my team who still types every answer from scratch. He's lovely, but he's slow. In a world where nothing much changes, he's fine too, it just means I get through more chats than him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worries at all in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the usual, like whether we can afford to buy a place before thirty. That's about house prices, not AI. Rhys and I check the listings on Sunday mornings and feel sad.

I'd tell coworkers to keep using it for the **boring bits**.
think: My **prompt list** keeps me ahead of colleagues who never learned AI.
My job feels **pretty safe** if the company keeps growing.
do: Share her **prompt list** with the team for credit.
Take a short online **bookkeeping course** to escalate less.
Keep saving towards **four months** put by.
feel: **Calm**, even a little **bored** by the idea.

fieldNote: She's a **daily AI user** who sees herself ahead of the curve.
Her real pressure is **house prices**, which she keeps separate from AI.
She wants to fix her weak spot in **accounting knowledge**.

steps.text: Share her personal prompt list with the support team
Take a short online bookkeeping course to escalate fewer tickets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers. Yes. That's me, very clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change things and the smart move is to get involved early. At work I'd say let's use it to clear the boring tickets and keep the interesting ones. I'd post about it, probably on a work networking site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, first-line support is exactly what gets automated, and I'm first-line. The bot will reset passwords and fix bank feeds better than I do. My only protection is being the person who helps build and check the bot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager this month if I can help write the bot's answers, because I already have my prompt list. I'd learn more about how these systems are trained, using free courses. I'd also look at the customer onboarding team, who do video calls to set up new businesses, which feels more human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in an active way. Like before an exam I've half revised for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company doesn't need you to build the bot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go somewhere that does. Plenty of small software firms will want someone who knows support and knows AI. I'm not attached to this company, I'm attached to paying rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guy who types everything from scratch. And my friend from school who works in a bank call centre and refuses to even try any of this. I've offered to show her, and she just changes the subject.

say: I'd say the smart move is to **get involved early**.
I'd post about it on a **work networking** site.
think: **First-line support** is exactly what gets automated, and I'm first-line.
My only protection is helping **build the bot**.
do: Ask her manager this month to help **write the bot's answers**.

Look at moving to the **onboarding team** for video set-up calls.
feel: **Anxious**, but active, like before a **half-revised exam**.

fieldNote: She sees her job as **first in line** and plans to move toward the bot.
Her loyalty is to **income**, not the employer.

steps.text: Ask her manager to help write the support bot's answers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that knocks the wind out of me a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments and companies working together, fast, or a lot of people get hurt. I'd say it without drama, because drama doesn't help. Online I'd share practical things, like which courses are free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, if AI can do almost any thinking work, my bot-building idea lasts maybe a year. Everything I'm good at is on a screen. The three-year gap before robots matters, so I'd need something hands-on, and I've never done hands-on work in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the next two years, I'd sell my AI set-up skills on the side to small business owners, because they'll all be scrambling. That money would pay for a dental nurse course, which I've looked at before, about a year part time. I'd stop the house deposit savings growing and keep them as an emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Excited by the tech and scared of what it does to me at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Dental nurse is a big jump. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt does it and she loves it. It's hands-on and it's with people. Nobody wants a robot near their mouth any time soon, and dental nursing is a short course, which matters when you've only got two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens with the house plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On hold. Rhys's job at the school is probably safer than mine, but we wouldn't buy anything on one teacher's wage. We'd sit down and redo our budget the same week.

say: I'd say governments and companies must **work together fast**.
I'd share **practical things**, like which courses are free.
think: My **bot-building plan** lasts maybe a year at most.
Everything I'm good at is **on a screen**, so I need hands-on work.
do: Sell **AI set-up help** to small business owners on the side.
Use that money for a **dental nurse** course.
Freeze the **house deposit** and keep it as an emergency fund.
S2.quote: Nobody wants a robot near their mouth any time soon, and dental nursing is a short course, which matters when you've only got two years.
fieldNote: She sees the **thinking-first** order clearly and moves to hands-on work.
She'd **profit from the scramble** to fund her switch.
The **house plan** stops, though her partner's job feels safer.

steps.text: Sell AI set-up help to small business customers on the side

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's tight, but it's workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a window, so people should start now and not wait for permission. At work I'd run a lunchtime session showing people how to use the tools. I'd say the government should fund short courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd get two or three good years building bots and doing AI set-ups, maybe even a pay rise. Then by 2031 that dries up. I'd want a hands-on skill ready by then, since robots don't come till about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd join the bot project at work and start a small side business setting up AI for local shops. I'd save the side money separately. In year two or three I'd start the dental nurse course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd teach colleagues. Why bother if you're leaving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want people to remember me as helpful. Some of my colleagues won't move unless someone shows them. Also, honestly, it looks good when I ask for the bot job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rhys?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm going to be busy for a few years and he might have to cook more. He'd be fine with that, he likes cooking. He'd worry I'm taking on too much.

say: I'd say people should **start now**, not wait for permission.
I'd run a **lunchtime session** on the tools for colleagues.
think: I'd get two or three **good years** building bots, maybe with a **pay rise**.
I'd need a **hands-on skill** ready before robots around 2034.
do: Join the **bot project** at work in the first year.

S3.quote: Some of my colleagues won't move unless someone shows them. Also, honestly, it looks good when I ask for the bot job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's comfortable. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to plan properly, and that people who start learning now will be fine. I'd say it at work and online. I'd also say the end point is the same, so don't get lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the next few years would be good for me. I'd be one of the AI people at work and could earn more. I'd only start worrying around 2032 or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for the bot job and ask for a raise within a year. I'd put the extra into a proper investment account, not just savings, so we can buy a place sooner. I'd keep an eye on the dental nurse idea for later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than worried. I know where it ends, but it's far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said don't get lazy. Is that advice for yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. Ten years is enough time to get comfortable and forget. I'd set myself a reminder for 2030 to check where things are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about this future excite you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Building things with these tools. I'd love a few years of being the person who makes the work better. I just know it won't last forever.

say: I'd say people who **start learning now** will be fine.
I'd add that the **end point** is the same, so nobody should get lazy.
think: The next few years would be **good for me** as one of the AI people.

Set a **2030 reminder** to reassess the dental nurse plan.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than worried, since the end point feels **far away**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even people like me who use AI every day would have nowhere to go. What would help is cheap, short courses for hands-on jobs, and some kind of support while you train.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the people who refuse to learn any of this. My friend at the bank won't even look at the tools. People who refuse to learn the tools need someone sitting next to them, not a website.

headlineQuote: People who refuse to learn the tools need someone sitting next to them, not a website.
portrait: Dana is 27 and does **first-line support** for small-business accounting software.

Her weak spot is **accounting knowledge**, so she escalates too much.
She plans to ride the **AI boom** first, then move to **dental nursing**.
She's pragmatic and loyal to **paying rent**, not to any employer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even daily AI users would have nowhere to go.
whatWouldHelp: **Support while training**, so people can afford to switch.
